title: Process model and a connection lifecycle
one_liner: One parent process (postmaster) listens and forks a new backend process per client, plus helper processes that do background chores.
analogy: A restaurant host seats each guest with their own waiter, while kitchen staff work quietly in the back. If the host panics, everyone resets.
big_picture: The postmaster is the parent. It listens on a socket, forks children, and restarts them if they die.
Each client connection gets its own backend process, forked from the postmaster. No threads per connection.
Helper processes do chores: checkpointer, bgwriter, walwriter and the startup process (recovery). Autovacuum workers and walsenders are other process types, started on demand.
All processes share one block of shared memory. The postmaster avoids locks and shared data structures, so a broken child cannot hang it.
A backend first reads a startup packet, then authenticates, then loops in PostgresMain reading messages.
Clients talk the frontend/backend protocol: one-letter message types like Q (simple query) or P/B/E (extended).

flow.detail: Reads config, sets up shared memory, opens listen sockets, starts the startup process and helpers.
The main loop waits on listen sockets and signals. When a client connects, it accepts the socket.
The postmaster takes a child slot, then forks a child of the right type. The child inherits shared memory.
flow.where: src/backend/postmaster/pmchild.c: assign_backend_pmchild; postmaster.c: BackendStartup; launch_backend.c: postmaster_child_launch

flow.step: Read startup packet, pick auth rule
flow.detail: The child learns protocol version, user and database. It then matches pg_hba.conf to choose the auth method.
The child gets a PGPROC slot (InitProcess). InitPostgres then runs ClientAuthentication, which runs the method chosen in the previous step.
BackendMain calls PostgresMain. It sends ReadyForQuery, then reads one command at a time with ReadCommand.
Simple protocol: exec_simple_query parses, plans and runs. Extended: Parse, Bind, Execute are separate messages.
On Terminate or EOF the backend exits. Postmaster sees SIGCHLD and cleans up the slot, or resets everything after a crash.

diagram.claim: A client connects to the postmaster, which forks a backend that authenticates and loops on queries, while helper processes share memory.

interview.q: Does PostgreSQL use threads or processes per connection?
answer: Processes. The postmaster forks one backend per client.
Processes isolate crashes and memory, but cost more than threads.
interview.trap: Many assume threads like MySQL. Postgres uses fork, not a thread pool.

interview.q: What does the postmaster do, and what does it avoid doing?
answer: It listens, forks children, and restarts them after exit.
It stays away from shared memory contents so it cannot be corrupted by a buggy child.
Look at ServerLoop in postmaster.c.

interview.q: Name the auxiliary processes and what each does.
answer: Auxiliary processes: checkpointer writes dirty pages at checkpoints, bgwriter trickles dirty pages out early, walwriter flushes WAL, startup replays WAL in recovery.
Autovacuum launcher asks the postmaster to start worker processes that vacuum tables.
A walsender is a normal backend running in replication mode. It streams WAL to a replica.
interview.trap: Calling walsender or autovacuum "auxiliary". Only startup, bgwriter, checkpointer, walwriter and a few more are.

interview.q: How does a client connect, step by step?
answer: A client connects. The postmaster accepts, then BackendStartup forks a child.
The child reads the startup packet in ProcessStartupPacket.
It matches pg_hba.conf (hba_getauthmethod), gets a PGPROC slot, then InitPostgres runs ClientAuthentication.
PostgresMain then sends ReadyForQuery.
interview.trap: Authentication happens in the child backend, not in the postmaster.

answer: hba.c matches connection type, database, user and address against pg_hba.conf.
This happens in BackendInitialize, right after the startup packet is read.
The first matching line names the method, such as scram-sha-256 or trust.
auth.c later runs that method, for example via auth-scram.c.

interview.q: What does PostgresMain do in its loop?
answer: It sets up signals and calls InitPostgres.
Then it repeats: send ReadyForQuery, ReadCommand, switch on the message type.
Q goes to exec_simple_query. P, B, E go to the extended handlers. X exits.
Simple: one Q message with SQL text. Server parses, plans and runs it all.
Extended: Parse, Bind, Execute, Sync as separate messages.
This allows prepared statements, parameters and binary formats.
interview.trap: Extended is not just faster. Its main value is safe parameters and reuse.

interview.q: What happens when one backend crashes?
answer: Postmaster sees the exit in process_pm_child_exit and calls HandleFatalError.
It signals all other children to quit, because shared memory may be corrupt.
Then it re-initializes and restarts, if restart_after_crash is on.
interview.trap: People think only the crashed connection dies. Every connection is dropped.

contributor_tips: Start by reading the header comment of postmaster.c, then follow BackendStartup into BackendMain.
Use a debugger: attach to a backend pid and break at PostgresMain or exec_simple_query.
Be careful: code run before fork or in the postmaster must not take locks or touch shared state.
Good first patches: docs, comments, tests under src/test, small protocol or error message fixes.

The per-connection process that runs a client's queries.

First message from client with user, database and protocol version.
A running query's state, created by Bind and run by Execute.

more: What happens at max_connections? The postmaster refuses with "too many clients".
Name the shutdown modes: smart, fast and immediate (SIGTERM, SIGINT, SIGQUIT).
How does query cancel work? A separate connection sends a cancel key to the postmaster.
Process per connection is costly. The usual answer is a pooler such as pgbouncer.
